# Solid State Battery Timelines for 2027 and Beyond

Solid-state batteries promise more range, faster charging and better safety. Here’s the realistic timeline for when they actually arrive, company by company.

Solid-state batteries are the most hyped technology in the EV world, and for years the running joke has been that they are always three years away. That is finally starting to change, but not in the way the headlines suggest. The realistic picture is a phased rollout: pilot production now, a handful of expensive low-volume vehicles near 2027 and 2028, and mainstream affordability clustered near 2030 and later. Here is what solid-state batteries actually change, and a grounded, company-by-company look at when they arrive.

!

Rimac Technology

## What solid-state actually changes

Today’s lithium-ion batteries use a liquid electrolyte, the flammable medium that carries ions between the electrodes. A solid-state battery replaces that liquid with a solid material, usually a ceramic or a sulfide compound. That single swap unlocks three big gains. Energy density rises sharply: current lithium-ion packs land near 250 to 300 watt-hours per kilogram, while solid-state cells target 400 to 500, close to double the energy in the same weight, which means more range or a lighter, smaller pack. Charging gets faster, with several developers targeting a 10% to 80% fill in under 10 minutes. And safety improves, because a solid electrolyte is far less prone to the fires that plague damaged liquid cells.

The catch is manufacturing. Building solid-state cells reliably and affordably at massive scale has proven extraordinarily difficult, which is why the technology has stayed perpetually on the horizon. The companies below are the ones now closest to solving it.

## The realistic phased timeline

Before the specifics, set expectations. Across the industry, the pattern is consistent: pilot and sample production in the mid-2020s, the first cars with solid-state or near-solid-state cells arriving in low volumes and at premium prices near 2027 and 2028, and genuine mass-market adoption, meaning affordable cars, not landing until near 2030 and beyond. If you are buying an EV between now and 2030, you are almost certainly buying a lithium-ion car, and that is fine, because those batteries are more affordable and better than ever.

## Toyota: the most aggressive automaker

Toyota has invested more than $15 billion and holds more solid-state patents than any other company, and it received formal production approval in Japan in late 2025. It is targeting its first all-solid-state EV for 2027 to 2028, using a sulfide electrolyte, with first-generation cells aimed at more than 600 miles of range and a 10% to 80% charge in under 10 minutes. Toyota also claims an unusually long service life, with cells retaining most of their capacity after decades. Those first vehicles will likely debut on premium Lexus models before the technology filters down.

## QuantumScape: the startup with the numbers

Backed by Volkswagen, QuantumScape has published some of the strongest verified lab results, with its QSE-5 cells hitting 844 watt-hours per liter and charging 10% to 80% in near 12 minutes. The company installed equipment for its automated Cobra production line in early 2026 and is targeting mass production in the 2027 to 2028 window. Its lithium-metal anode design, which eliminates the graphite layer in conventional cells, is central to its energy-density advantage.

## Samsung SDI: premium first

Samsung SDI has demonstrated cells with 900 watt-hours per liter, nearly double current lithium-ion, and is targeting 2027 for limited production, initially for premium vehicles. It has partnered with BMW and Solid Power to co-develop and validate cells using a sulfide electrolyte, and it aims for an 80% charge in near nine minutes. It has run a pilot line since 2023 and already supplies partners with semi-solid cells.

## The rest of the field

Others are close behind on similar timelines. Nissan is targeting a 2028 commercial launch of its own solid-state production. BMW, working with Samsung SDI and Solid Power, is validating cells in demonstration vehicles. Mercedes-Benz has road-tested a prototype pack, driving an EQS nearly 750 miles on a charge, but plans commercial introduction only in the early 2030s. Honda is running its own demonstration line with Factorial Energy, aiming for the late 2020s. And battery giant CATL plans semi-solid cells near 2026 with full solid-state closer to 2030.

## The catches: cost, scale and marketing

Two cautions are worth keeping in mind. The first is cost. Every credible timeline points to premium vehicles first, with cost parity against lithium-ion, and therefore affordable solid-state cars, not arriving until near 2030. The technology will trickle down exactly the way lithium-ion once did, from flagships to the mainstream over years.

The second is language. The term solid-state is used loosely, and many announcements actually describe semi-solid cells that still contain a small amount of liquid electrolyte. These are easier to build and are shipping sooner, but they do not deliver the full promised leap in energy density and safety of a true all-solid-state cell. When you read a timeline, it pays to check which one a company actually means.

## What it means for buyers

If you are shopping for an EV in the next few years, solid-state batteries should not make you wait. The first vehicles that use them will be expensive, low-volume, premium models arriving near 2027 and 2028, and the affordable ones are the better part of a decade away. Meanwhile, today’s lithium-ion EVs keep improving, with more affordable LFP chemistry, silicon-anode range gains, and steady manufacturing efficiencies pushing prices down. A lithium-ion car bought today has a long, useful life ahead of it.

The bottom line is that solid-state batteries are real, they are finally reaching production, and they will genuinely transform range, charging and safety when they mature. But the transition will be gradual, premium-first, and measured in years, not months. The technology is arriving on schedule for once; just expect it to reach the driveway of an average buyer near 2030, not 2027.
